overview: A two-page State Department list of papers for file 894.76, summarizing records on Japanese wireless telephony and radio broadcasting during 1940. The listed material chiefly concerns arrangements for a July 5 trans-Pacific tribute to the late Prince Iyesato Tokugawa, including Ambassador Joseph C. Grew’s participation and the proposed rebroadcast in the United States; it also covers Japanese overseas shortwave programming, an American broadcast by Count Kobayashi, restrictions on foreign merchant ships’ radio equipment at Yokohama, and plans to expand Japanese international broadcasting, including Portuguese-language service.

subfiles.title: List of Papers: Wireless Telephone in Japan
subfiles.about: An archival contents list summarizes 1940 correspondence and reports concerning Japanese domestic and overseas radio broadcasting and wartime radio controls.
subfiles.summary: The first page lists telegrams, letters, and despatches concerning the July 5, 1940 broadcast tribute to Prince Iyesato Tokugawa, including arrangements by Viscount Inouye, Ambassador Grew’s proposed remarks, State Department approval, and plans for an American rebroadcast. It also identifies reports on Japanese shortwave programming, Count Kobayashi’s broadcast to the United States, and the sealing of transmitting equipment aboard foreign merchant ships in Yokohama harbor. The second page records a pamphlet about the Tokugawa tribute and later reports on the development and planned expansion of Japanese overseas broadcasting, including a partially illegible note about Portuguese-language service.

interest: The list is useful as a compact roadmap to a larger diplomatic file, revealing how cultural commemoration, public diplomacy, commercial broadcasting, and wartime communications regulation intersected in 1940. Of particular interest are the coordination among Ambassador Grew, Japanese officials, the Federal Communications Commission, and the National Broadcasting Company for a trans-Pacific memorial broadcast, and the simultaneous monitoring of Japan’s expanding multilingual overseas radio service. The Yokohama entry also points to early wartime controls imposed on radio transmitters aboard foreign merchant vessels after the outbreak of war in Europe.
